ratha
(‘that which delights,’ ‘chariot’)
------------------------------------------
The रथ or the chariot—a carriage with two wheels and drawn by two or more horses—was quite common even during the times of the Ṛgveda (vide 1.20.3; 3.15.5; 6.75 and so on). It was used widely not only as a means of transportation but also in wars. Fabricating rathas was a highly specialised job assigned to the rathakāras. The Viṣṇu-dharmottarapurāṇa gives many details regarding the manufacture of rathas. Descriptions of the various kinds of rathas of the different deities, symbolical interpretations based on them, interesting accounts of expert sārathis or charioteers like अरुण and Mātali are often found in the epics and the पुराणस्.
Works like the Mānasāra, the Śilparatnākara and the Rudravāstu give details about their design and building as also the materials suitable for making them. Different kinds of rathas such as puṣparatha, vimānaratha, somyaratha and gandharvaratha are also mentioned.
The number of wheels also varies—from two to ten—depending on the use for which they are made.
They were normally drawn by horses, especially in wars or chariot-sports (including races). For transporting goods, even bullocks were harnessed.
Nowadays, the word ‘ratha’ is almost exclusively used to indicate the wooden chariots used in most of the temples, which are taken out on festive occasions. Such occasions are called Rathotsavas. They are annual events, the days chosen being the day of consecration of the temple or of the installation of the main icon. These rathas are generally prepared out of the wood called tiniśa (Dalbergia onjeinensis). They are often made artistically with lovely carvings.
There are elaborate rituals connected with the रथोत्सव, such as worshipping the रथ first, placing the deity on it, drawing it along the route fixed for its movement, taking the deity out at the end, and conducting it back to its shed.
The रथ symbolises the mount मेरु, the wheels stand for the sun and मोओन्, the images of the four horses carved on wood, for the four वेदस्, and, the charioteer represents the creator ब्रह्मा.
The word रथ may also stand for a variety of temple architecture as seen in the rathas of महाबलिपुरम्. (See MAHĀBALIPURAM for details.)

Rathayātrā
(‘moving the chariot’)
------------------------------------------
The रथयात्रा festival (Āṣāḍha śukla dvitīyā) of Lord Jagannātha at पुरी (in Orissa) is a world-renowned event drawing lakhs of people every year.
Rathayātrā at JagannāthapurīPurī or Jagannāthapurī is one of the four ‘dhāmas’ (important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे situated in the four cardinal directions of India), the other three being Badarī in the north (Uttar Pradesh), द्वारका in the west (Gujarat) and रामेश्वरम् in the south (Tamil Nadu). Known as the ‘Puruṣottama-क्षेत्र’ in the ancient days, the present temple of Lord Jagannātha is said to have been built by the king इन्द्र-dyumna. The temple with the wooden images of Śrī कृष्ण (Jagannātha), बल-bhadra (Balarāma, कृष्ण’s elder brother) and सुभद्रा (Kṛṣṇa’s younger sister) must have been in existence for over 1300 years. The wooden images are replaced periodically with new ones, the ‘relics’ inside the old ones being transferred to the new ones, before the former are disposed of according to the directions given in the concerned scriptures.
The पुरी जगन्नाथ तेम्प्ले is, perhaps, the only temple in India where the mūlavigrahas (original icons) themselves are shifted on to the rathas (chariots) for the रथोत्सव (chariot festival). In all other temples, there are separate icons, called ‘utsavamūrtis’, which are used for the रथोत्सव.
the रथोत्सव.In the रथयात्रा festival three rathas are used: One for Jagannātha, called Nandighoṣa, 13.5 metres (45 ft.) in height, with 16 wheels of 2.1 metres (7 ft.) diameter; the second for बलराम, called Tāladhvaja, 13.2 metres (44 ft.) in height with 14 wheels; and the third for सुभद्रा, called Devīratha or Darpa-dalana, 12.9 metres (43 ft.) in height and with 12 wheels.
After the ceremonial installation of the deities inside the chariots, it is the privilege of the king of पुरी (a descendant of Anantavarma [A.

-1150]) to sweep the chariot of the Lord and pay his homage. Then lakhs of devotees join in the pulling by big ropes, with shouts of ‘Jagannāthakī jay,’ ‘Balabhadrakī jay’ and Subhadrākī jay’. The procession stops at Guṇḍīcābārī, the garden होउसे of the deities. After a stay of seven days, the images are brought back to the main temple on the daśamī day.
The रथयात्रा (travel by the chariot) may be a ritual re-enactment of the journey of सुभद्रा, escorted by कृष्ण and बलराम, to द्वारका. As per the mythological lore, सुभद्रा expressed a desire to see the newly constructed city of द्वारका; and was accordingly taken there by her brothers.

rathotsava
(‘festival of the [temple] chariot’)
------------------------------------------
The biggest festival organised in any temple is called ‘brahmotsava’. It is generally spread over a number of days. The रथोत्सव is an important part of this festival and is usually held two days before the conclusion of all the ceremonies.
The रथ (temple-car or chariot) is a replica of the temple. It is richly decorated along with the उत्सवमूर्ति (processional image) and taken round the important streets of the town. It is halted in certain specified places so that the common people can offer their worship almost at their door-step.
The रथ is drawn by the devotees, no distinction being made of caste or creed.
Of course, there are a number of religious rites connected with the रथोत्सव, which should be observed scrupulously.

rathakāra
(‘one who builds a रथ [chariot]’)
------------------------------------------
A रथकार is actually a carpenter who has specialised in the art of preparing rathas or chariots. He has been mentioned as taṣṭā or त्वष्टा even in the Ṛgveda (vide 1.61.4; 8.102.8).
Since his services were essential in the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, he was given the status almost equal to that of a द्विज (the twice-born, the first three castes). Hence, he could undergo the उपनयन rite and even establish the Vedic fires.
Apart from the making of chariots, he could also live by taming horses, driving carts and building houses.
Gradually his status declined to that of a śūdra, thanks to the rigidity of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् of later periods.

Rathasaptamī
------------------------------------------
Those desirous of freedom from diseases and a robust health are advised to worship भास्कर or सूर्य, the sun. रथसप्तमी which falls on Māgha śukla saptamī (in February) is a vrata dedicated to the worship of the sun, to get that or fulfilment of any other desire. It consists of worship of the sun seated in a chariot—usually in image—with saffron and flowers, ड़स्तिन्ग् for the whole day, keeping vigil the whole night with devotional songs and मुसिच्. After bath next morning, gifts should be made to the गुरु (preceptor) and others.
Rathasaptamī—also called Acala-saptamī—is the day on which वैवस्वत-मन्वन्तर started, on which the sun was born and also the day on which he started going northward (uttarāyaṇa).
